## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds, so any reliable non-zero score is a real gain. Each step, the agent has to find a footprint where the brick lands at height z = max(build height under the footprint), and every cell it fills at layer z must be 'missing'. It must also avoid sealing missing cells underneath. The starting network gets the layers only as a flat channel stack and pools over footprints just once, so it has to discover this per-layer rule from scratch. The budget is small: 131k steps, about 32 updates at the default recipe. This round has three trials in a 2x2 design missing one cell. The first is a new layer-conditioned footprint head with the default recipe. The second is the starting network with a recipe that gives twice as many updates. The third combines both. Together they should show whether the architecture or the update count is the bottleneck. Because seed noise is high, I will treat differences under about 0.05 as inconclusive.

### Round 2
All four results are 0.000 on both seeds, and training success in the last 10% of each run is 0 too. So none of the agents ever learned to make an exact build, even while acting stochastically. The layer-conditioned head and doubling the number of updates (still 4 epochs) both made no difference. These results cannot rank the architectures. They do suggest that the agent sees too little data: about 131k steps is only around 4,000 episodes. The cheapest way to get more data is fewer PPO epochs. One epoch gives about 3.25x more environment samples, and 2 epochs about 1.86x. A second likely issue is the default output scale of the policy head. With up to about 257 legal actions, a small-gain output layer gives a near-uniform start, which tends to make PPO more stable. This round tests those recipe levers on the start net. The third candidate also tries a deeper per-cell column network, because finding where the next brick should go and whether a cell is still missing at the current build height is a non-trivial function of the column. The r1c1 layer head is too slow (252s for 131k steps) to run with 3x the samples.

### Round 3
All six trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on training, whatever the recipe (1 to 4 epochs, 131k to 426k steps, small output init) and whichever of the 2D nets was used. Changing the recipe alone does not help, so the bottleneck is probably what the network can see. An exact placement needs, at the landing layer z: every footprint cell missing at z, column height at most z (equal to z for at least one cell), and no missing cells below z. The 2D nets mix all layers in a 1x1 stem. r1c1's per-layer head used the same weights for every z plus a z-bias, so it could not pick out layer z's own channels. That is a likely bug, not a refutation of the per-layer idea. Fix: slice obs per layer (channels for z-1, z and z+1, plus heights and a z-position channel), use a shared learned per-cell MLP, then cumulative max over layers (below and above), then footprint pooling per layer. I test this at two recipes and with an added per-layer spatial conv.

### Round 4
All nine trials scored exactly 0 on dev, and training success was also 0 in every run. This held across three architecture families (the start net, the layer-conditioned head and the layer-sliced net) and across recipes (more updates, 1 or 2 epochs, 3x the samples, small output initialisation). Seed noise alone cannot explain this. A dense shaped reward with roughly 400k samples should give at least occasional exact builds, so something basic is probably broken. The task warns that the world may not match its description. One likely mismatch is that the action indexing is not aligned with the observation grid (transposed, flipped, or a different anchor). If so, every convolutional footprint head we tried puts each action's logit at the wrong cells, and a local convolution cannot learn that non-local shift. This last round tests that idea with heads that can learn any mapping from cells to actions.
